claim: MreB motion in B. subtilis rods remained equivalently oriented over a wide range of rod widths, up to ~2 μm.

claim: Beyond a 2 μm width, cells began to lose their rod shape as they became more spherical, and the predominantly circumferential orientation of MreB motion was lost.

claim: The orientation of MreB motion relies on differences between the two principal curvatures of the membrane.

claim: When TagO-depleted cells grew out of the microfluidic chamber they swelled, showing confinement was required for rod shape at this induction level.

claim: In TagO-depleted cells confined into rod shapes, MreB moved circumferentially.

claim: The isotropic MreB motion observed in round cells arises from the lack of rod shape, and not from some other effect of genetic perturbations.

claim: The doubling time of free TagO-depleted cells at similar induction levels is 53 ± 10 min.

claim: Confining TagO-depleted cells into rod shape restored their doubling time (44 ± 4 min) toward wild-type times (39 ± 9 min).

claim: MreB filaments within protoplasts did not move directionally.

claim: The cell wall provides the fixed surface along which the PG synthesis enzymes move.

claim: Within protoplasts confined into the smallest rod shapes (2 μm), MreB filaments oriented at a distribution of angles predominantly perpendicular to the cell length.

claim: Both short and long MreB filaments in spherically confined protoplasts remained unoriented.

evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MreB filaments orient to point around the rod width even in the absence of pre-existing cell wall or directional motion, as long as the cell has a rod shape.

claim: At the highest concentrations, tubulated liposomes contained closely packed filament bundles with a regular patterning of the canonical double filaments of MreB.

claim: Purified wild-type MreB did not bind to the outside surface of small liposomes contained within larger ones.
source: Purified wild-type MreB did not bind to the outside surface of small liposomes contained within larger ones (Figure 4A), indicating that MreB filaments preferentially polymerize on inward (negative) curvatures, akin to the inner leaflet of the bacterial membrane.

claim: MreB filaments preferentially polymerize on inward (negative) curvatures, akin to the inner leaflet of the bacterial membrane.

claim: In the absence of MreB, liposomes are spherical, with no deformations.

source: These calculations indicate that the total energy is minimized when filaments orient along the direction of maximal curvature (Figure 4F) and that, importantly, the energy penalty for incorrectly-oriented filaments is much greater than the energy of thermal fluctuations.

source: These calculations indicate that the total energy is minimized when filaments orient along the direction of maximal curvature (Figure 4F) and that, importantly, the energy penalty for incorrectly-oriented filaments is much greater than the energy of thermal fluctuations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: MreB filament orientation is robust over a large, biologically relevant range of parameters, including membrane binding energy, filament length, and filament Young's modulus.
source: Furthermore, our calculations indicate that orientation is robust over a large, biologically relevant range of parameters, including the membrane binding energy, filament length, and filament Young's modulus (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling stated in the text and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Calculations predict that filaments should orient circumferentially both if the membrane deforms to the filament or if filaments deform to the membrane.
source: These calculations predict that filaments should orient circumferentially both if the membrane deforms to the filament (at low osmotic pressures or if filaments are stiff) (Salje et al., 2011), or if filaments deform to the membrane (at high osmotic pressures or if filaments are flexible) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Experimental data demonstrates MreB filament alignment across a range of pressures: high within cells, low to none within liposomes, and a pressure between the two within osmotically-stabilized protoplasts.
source: Our experimental data demonstrates MreB filament alignment across a range of pressures: high within cells, low to none within liposomes, and a pressure between the two within osmotically-stabilized protoplasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

source: In the absence of osmotic pressure, MreB filaments deform liposomes since it is energetically more favorable to bend the membranes than to bend the filaments, as observed in our in vitro data (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling and in vitro data.

claim: In live cells, modeling predicts that MreB filaments cannot deform the inner membrane due to the large osmotic pressure, and instead deform to match the greatest principal membrane curvature.
source: However, in live cells, our modeling predicts that MreB filaments cannot deform the inner membrane due to the large osmotic pressure, and instead deform to match the greatest principal membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: MreB filaments create curvature in liposomes and sense it in cells.
source: Hence filaments create curvature in liposomes and sense it in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling and experimental data.

evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells grown at intermediate TagO induction levels (8-12 mM) grew as steady state populations of interconnected rods and spheres, indicating repeated cycles of rod shape formation followed by reversion to spheres.
source: Likewise, cells grown at intermediate TagO induction levels (8–12 mM) grew as steady state populations of interconnected rods and spheres, indicating that cells underwent repeated cycles of rod shape formation followed by reversion to spheres (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: Rod shape can be maintained only as long as the cell wall is sufficiently rigid to resist the internal osmotic pressure.
source: These results indicate that rod shape can be maintained only as long as the cell wall is sufficiently rigid to resist the internal osmotic pressure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

source: Increases in expression of tagO or pbpA from depleted spherical cells causes cells to emit rapidly elongating rods from discrete points.

source: By examining the initial time points of recoveries, we found that rods begin as small outward bulges: local regions of outward (positive Gaussian) curvature flanked by regions of inward (negative Gaussian) curvature (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Initial outward bulges showed a width distribution similar to that of the later emerging rods.
source: These initial outward bulges showed a width distribution similar to that of the later emerging rods (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

source: Once these bulges formed, they immediately began rapid elongation into nascent rods, which would then thin down to wild type width over time.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text.

source: Bulge formation and rod recovery were independent of cell division, as cells depleted of FtsZ still recovered rod shape (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The appearance of a local outward bulge can act as the nucleating event of rod shape formation.
source: We conclude that the appearance of a local outward bulge can act as the nucleating event of rod shape formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: There is a sharp transition in doubling time that matches the conditions of the rod/sphere transition: growth is slow when cells are spheres, yet greatly increases when cells are rods.
source: This revealed a sharp transition in doubling time that matched the conditions of the rod/sphere transition: growth is slow when cells are spheres, yet greatly increases when cells are rods (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The doubling times of recovering rods was similar to that of rods at steady state.
source: Furthermore, the doubling times of recovering rods was similar to that of rods at steady state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The lower doubling time of rods is likely due to cell shape and not another effect, such as the lack of WTAs.
source: We believe the lower doubling time of rods is likely due to cell shape and not another effect, such as the lack of WTAs, as (1) the doubling time of TagO-depleted cells confined in the microfluidic chambers matched that of wild type cells; and (2) both the doubling times and the boundary of the rod/sphere transition could be equivalently shifted by changing the Mg2+ concentration (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Rod shape creates local, self-reinforcing regions that are poised for more rapid growth.
source: Combined, these results indicate that rod shape creates local, self-reinforcing regions that are poised for more rapid growth; once any small region of the cell approximates a rod shape, growth of the rod-like region is amplified, growing faster than other regions, and thereby outcompeting non-rod growth at the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Emerging rods displayed oriented MreB motion even at the initial points of their formation, while attached round parent cells displayed unaligned motion.
source: This revealed that oriented MreB motion correlates with local shape: emerging rods displayed oriented MreB motion even at the initial points of their formation, while attached round parent cells displayed unaligned motion (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Oriented MreB motion correlates with local geometry and does not arise from a global, cell spanning change.
source: This demonstrates that oriented MreB motion correlates with local geometry and does not arise from a global, cell spanning change.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Immediately prior to rod emergence, MreB transiently accumulated in a bright ring oriented perpendicular to the direction of rod emergence, most often occurring at the interface of the bulge and the round cells.
source: We next examined the overall cellular distribution of MreB in recovering cells with confocal microscopy. This revealed that, immediately prior to rod emergence, MreB transiently accumulated in a bright ring oriented perpendicular to the direction of rod emergence, most often occurring at the interface of the bulge and the round cells (Figure 6B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both spheres and rods incorporate new cell wall material during rod shape recovery.
source: During rod emergence, the old cell wall signal (HADA) remained in the sphere, while the emerging rod was almost entirely composed of new (Cy3B-ADA) material, confirming the discrete nature of rod shape recovery. However, the attached spheres also incorporated Cy3B-ADA, indicating PG synthesis occurs in both rods and spheres during recovery (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: WTAs in recovering cells were equally present in the cell walls of both rods and spheres.
source: Following TagO reinduction, WTAs in recovering cells were (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), equally present in the cell walls of both rods and spheres (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WTA ligases appeared to be rapidly diffusing on the membrane, not moving with MreB.
source: To test if the WTA ligases move with MreB, we created GFP fusions to these proteins at their native locus and examined their dynamics with TIRFM. We were unable to observe any of the circumferential motions expected if the WTA ligases moved with MreB; instead they appeared to be rapidly diffusing on the membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Figure 6—video 2, Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Single molecule tracking did not observe any directional motions of the WTA ligases that would indicate they move or associate with MreB and Pbp2A.
source: For further confirmation, we tracked the single molecule motions of these ligases, using JF549 labeled HaloTag fusions expressed at the native locus and promoter. We did not observe any directional motions of the ligases that would indicate they move or associate with MreB and Pbp2A (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E, Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: The only differences detected between rod shaped and round cells were increased growth rates and oriented MreB motion.
source: In summary, these data gives new insights into what properties of the cell wall can be modulated to create and stabilize rod shape: rod shape is not formed by preferential localization of teichoic acids to rods, and both spheres and rods incorporate PG before and during rod shape recovery, in line with reports that PG synthesis is unchanged by the inhibition of WTA synthesis (Pooley et al., 1993). Rather, the only differences we detected between rod shaped and round cells were increased growth rates and oriented MreB motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: PG synthesis is unchanged by the inhibition of WTA synthesis.
source: In summary, these data gives new insights into what properties of the cell wall can be modulated to create and stabilize rod shape: rod shape is not formed by preferential localization of teichoic acids to rods, and both spheres and rods incorporate PG before and during rod shape recovery, in line with reports that PG synthesis is unchanged by the inhibition of WTA synthesis (Pooley et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The curved ultrastructure of MreB filaments causes them to orient and move along the direction of greatest membrane curvature, inserting material in that direction.
source: First, the curved ultrastructure of MreB filaments causes them to orient and move along the direction of greatest membrane curvature, inserting material in that direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: Both the formation and propagation of rod shape occurs by a local, self-reinforcing process.
source: Second, both the formation and propagation of rod shape occurs by a local, self-reinforcing process: once a local region of rod shape forms, it propagates more rod shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: The primary differences between the growth of rods and non-rods is the circumferential orientation of MreB motion.
source: Finally, as far as we can determine, the primary differences between the growth of rods and non-rods is the circumferential orientation of MreB motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: MreB filaments function as curvature-sensing rudders.
source: Combined, these findings indicate that MreB filaments function as curvature-sensing rudders, a property that allows them to organize cell wall synthesis so that it builds rod shape: MreB filaments orient along the greatest membrane principal curvature, thereby constraining the activity of the associated PG synthases so that, as they move via their synthetic activity, they deposit glycans oriented in the direction of that curvature, an arrangement of material that further reinforces rod shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: Even during the initial stages of rod shape formation, oriented MreB motion and rod shape always coincide.
source: Even during the initial stages of rod shape formation, oriented MreB motion and rod shape always coincide, and the intrinsic curvature of MreB filaments suggests these properties cannot be uncoupled.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: The intrinsic curvature of MreB filaments suggests oriented motion and rod shape cannot be uncoupled.
source: Even during the initial stages of rod shape formation, oriented MreB motion and rod shape always coincide, and the intrinsic curvature of MreB filaments suggests these properties cannot be uncoupled.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: By linking filaments that orient along the greatest principal curvature to cell wall synthetic enzymes reinforcing that curvature, the Rod complex may function as a local, self-organizing system.
source: This coupling appears to be an essential component of the Rod system: by linking filaments that orient along the greatest principal curvature to cell wall synthetic enzymes reinforcing that curvature, the Rod complex may function as a local, self-organizing system that allows bacteria to both maintain rod shape and also establish rod shape de novo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: MreB maintains and propagates rod shape via a local feedback between existing shape, filament orientation, and subsequent shape-reinforcing PG synthesis.
source: In established rods, we propose that MreB maintains and propagates rod shape via a local feedback between existing shape, filament orientation, and subsequent shape-reinforcing PG synthesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: The circumferential insertion of glycan strands yields an anisotropic arrangement of material that reinforces rod shape.
source: This circumferential insertion of glycan strands would yield an anisotropic arrangement of material that reinforces rod shape (Figure 7A1), allowing for continued MreB filament orientation.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Once the rod is formed, the feedback loop allows robust shape maintenance, as long as the material within the rod sidewalls is sufficiently rigid to withstand the stresses arising from osmotic pressure.
source: Once the rod is formed, this feedback loop allows robust shape maintenance, as long as the material within the rod sidewalls is sufficiently rigid to withstand the stresses arising from osmotic pressure.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: The MreB guided circumferential insertion of cell wall material is expected to reinforce rod shape.
source: While the MreB guided circumferential insertion of cell wall material is expected to reinforce rod shape (Amir and Nelson, 2012; Chang and Huang, 2014; Baskin, 2005), it must be noted that it is not sufficient, as other factors are also needed: WTA-depleted cells become round (D'Elia et al., 2006) (Figure 1D) even under conditions where they contain oriented MreB motions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations, and confirmed by the current data.

claim: WTAs, in combination with PG, work to coordinate Mg2+ to increase the overall cell wall stiffness.
source: Based on both past work (Matias and Beveridge, 2005; Kern et al., 2010) and our data (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 2), we believe that WTAs, in combination with PG, work to coordinate Mg2+ to increase the overall cell wall stiffness, thus allowing regions of oriented insertion to maintain and propagate their shape.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior studies and the current data.

claim: The coupling between the local sensing and reinforcement of differences in principal curvature could facilitate the de novo formation of rod shape.
source: The coupling between the local sensing and reinforcement of differences in principal curvature could also facilitate the de novo formation of rod shape.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: The Rod system appears poised to propagate any shape variations that create curved regions favorable to oriented MreB motion.
source: Given the rapid timescale of our recoveries, the Rod system appears poised to propagate any shape variations that create curved regions favorable to oriented MreB motion: as soon as regions of oriented motion are established, they self-propagate and elongate, creating more rod shape and thus continued oriented MreB motion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The geometry at the interface of outward bulges and spheres may play a nucleating role in rod shape formation.
source: Whether these outward bulges arise from physical effects or by the action of upstream factors, the geometry at their interface may play a nucleating role in rod shape formation.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: The intersection of the bulge and the sphere creates an interface with large differences in principal curvatures, one inward, and one outward (negative Gaussian curvature).
source: In three dimensions, the intersection of the bulge and the sphere creates a geometry that can establish a zone of aligned filaments: while both the parent sphere and the outward bulge have principal curvatures in the same direction (positive Gaussian curvature), the intersection of the sphere and bulge creates an interface with large differences in principal curvatures, one inward, and one outward (negative Gaussian curvature).
evidence: This is an inference based on geometric considerations.

claim: Upon entering negatively curved regions at the bulge neck, it is energetically unfavorable for the inwardly curved MreB filaments to deviate from their preferred binding orientation.
source: Upon entering these negatively curved regions it is energetically unfavorable for the inwardly curved MreB filaments to deviate from their preferred binding orientation, as our modeling indicates that this region presents a steep well in the energy profile for alignment (Figure 7B2 and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling and shown in Figure 7B2.

claim: Filaments moving into the bulge neck rim from either side would reorient to move along it, creating a concentrated band of filaments moving around the bulge neck.
source: Thus, filaments moving into this rim from either side would reorient to move along it, creating a concentrated band of filaments moving around the bulge neck.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 7B3.

source: In support of this hypothesis, immediately preceding rod shape formation, we observe concentrated bands of MreB transiently appearing at the neck of emerging bulges (Figure 6B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.
